cards.noteEn: Wifi is used as a Spanish noun. It is often feminine because red, 'network,' is understood: la wifi. Usage and pronunciation vary by region.

example.es: La wifi del hotel es lenta.

cards.noteEn: Buscar already includes the idea expressed by English ‘for.’ Spanish normally puts the sought item directly after buscar, without adding por.

example.en: I am looking for my keys.

cards.noteEn: For a wireless network, abierta means that access is not protected by a password. The feminine plural form abiertas agrees with redes.

example.en: There are two open networks here.

cards.answerEn: found (feminine singular, in a status message)
cards.noteEn: Encontrada is the feminine singular result form of encontrar, ‘to find.’ A short status message can omit a full verb such as se ha and simply report encontrada before or after a feminine noun.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.
Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.
Colegio commonly means a primary or secondary school. It does not normally mean a university-level college.

example.es: Mi colegio está cerca de casa.
example.en: My school is close to home.

cards.answerEn: found (masculine plural, in a status message)
cards.noteEn: Encontrados is the masculine plural result form of encontrar, ‘to find.’ In a terse status message it agrees with a masculine or mixed plural noun even when the full expression se han encontrado is omitted.
Hijos can mean sons, but the masculine plural also commonly refers to a group of children that includes a daughter.

example.es: Tienen un hijo y una hija: dos hijos en total.
example.en: They have a son and a daughter: two children in total.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

cards.answerEn: field; work done on location rather than in an office
cards.noteEn: After a profession, de campo describes practical work carried out where events happen. English usually puts field before the profession instead.

example.es: Ella es una investigadora de campo.

cards.noteEn: Niños can refer specifically to boys or more generally to a group of children whose members are male or mixed. The surrounding context decides which meaning is intended.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio.
example.en: The children are playing in the yard.

cards.noteEn: Obtenidos reports a completed result and agrees with a masculine plural noun. Using obtener for people sounds deliberately cold and bureaucratic; it is more ordinary with things such as documents or results.
